frictionVectors.title: European Gas Dependence
frictionVectors.details: Algeria retains bargaining power as a major gas supplier to Europe, but export infrastructure and long-term contracts expose it to external pricing and demand shifts.

frictionVectors.title: Foreign Energy Partnerships
frictionVectors.details: Italian, American, and other foreign firms remain important in upstream investment, creating periodic tension over technology access, contract terms, and domestic control.

frictionVectors.title: Critical-Mineral Corridor Rivalry
frictionVectors.details: The Lobito Corridor is attracting US, European, Gulf, and Chinese interest, giving Angola infrastructure leverage but increasing competition over future copper, cobalt, and logistics rents.

frictionVectors.title: Debt-Linked Oil Exposure
frictionVectors.details: Oil revenues remain central to fiscal stability, while debt obligations and foreign participation in production limit Luanda's room to direct resource income toward domestic diversification.

frictionVectors.title: Niger Trade Disruption
frictionVectors.details: Relations with Niger continue to affect the strategic value of Cotonou's port and regional transit networks, with sanctions legacies and border insecurity constraining trade.

frictionVectors.title: External Infrastructure Finance
frictionVectors.details: Chinese, European, and regional financing supports roads, energy, and port expansion, but repayment terms and foreign operating roles remain sensitive sovereignty issues.

frictionVectors.title: De Beers Negotiation Pressure
frictionVectors.details: Botswana is pressing for greater value capture, sorting, and downstream participation in its diamond sector as market weakness tests the balance with De Beers.

frictionVectors.title: Mineral Diversification Race
frictionVectors.details: Foreign investors are targeting copper, nickel, and other minerals, creating opportunities for diversification while raising concerns over licensing terms and local beneficiation.

frictionVectors.title: Foreign Gold-Refining Influence
frictionVectors.details: The junta is seeking tighter state control over gold production, refining, and sales, challenging established foreign operators and informal networks while raising enforcement risks.

frictionVectors.title: Russian Security Dependence
frictionVectors.details: Expanded security cooperation with Russia offers an alternative to Western influence but may increase opaque access to mining concessions and deepen dependence on an external security partner.

highlights: Gold and Critical-Mineral Governance Under Pressure

frictionVectors.title: Informal Mining and Cross-Border Smuggling
frictionVectors.details: Gold and coltan revenues remain vulnerable to informal extraction and illicit routes through neighboring states. Limited regulatory capacity reduces the government's ability to convert mineral wealth into public revenue.

frictionVectors.title: Rwanda-Burundi Security Friction
frictionVectors.details: Mutual accusations and armed-group activity along the border disrupt trade and complicate regional infrastructure planning. Continued instability raises the cost of securing transport and energy links.

frictionVectors.title: External Control of Ports and Connectivity
frictionVectors.details: Foreign financing and operating partnerships support port, airport, and digital infrastructure but can narrow national policy space. Cabo Verde must balance European, Chinese, and other external commercial interests.

frictionVectors.title: Maritime Resource Security
frictionVectors.details: Illegal fishing and limited naval capacity threaten the value of the country's large maritime zone. Dependence on foreign surveillance and security assistance remains significant.

highlights: Oil, Gas, and Mining Revenue Under Strain

frictionVectors.title: Foreign Influence in Strategic Infrastructure
frictionVectors.details: Chinese and other external firms remain important in roads, mining, energy, and logistics, while financing arrangements can limit transparency over future revenues. Delays and cost overruns weaken state control over infrastructure assets.

frictionVectors.title: Anglophone Conflict and Resource Corridors
frictionVectors.details: Armed conflict in the Northwest and Southwest disrupts transport, agriculture, and local administration. Insecurity threatens planned energy and extractive projects and increases reliance on centralized security structures.

frictionVectors.title: Russian-Controlled Security and Mining Access
frictionVectors.details: The government's dependence on Russian security personnel has increased Moscow-linked leverage over political and commercial decisions. Gold and diamond arrangements remain opaque, limiting sovereign revenue capture.

frictionVectors.title: Weak Transport and Border Infrastructure
frictionVectors.details: Poor roads and insecurity leave the country dependent on neighboring states and external actors for trade access. Armed groups and cross-border networks continue to contest resource corridors.

frictionVectors.title: Foreign Leverage over Oil Infrastructure
frictionVectors.details: The economy remains concentrated around oil production and export infrastructure controlled or financed through international partnerships. Price volatility, contract disputes, and limited diversification weaken bargaining power.

frictionVectors.title: Sudan Border and Internal Security Pressure
frictionVectors.details: The war in Sudan is driving refugee flows, arms trafficking, and insecurity across eastern Chad. Military spending and border management divert resources from civilian infrastructure and broader economic sovereignty.

highlights: Aid and maritime dependence constrain autonomy

frictionVectors.title: Mayotte and maritime jurisdiction
frictionVectors.details: France retains control of Mayotte, sustaining a sovereignty dispute and complicating Comoros' access to surrounding maritime resources. Migration enforcement adds recurring diplomatic friction.

frictionVectors.title: External financing dependence
frictionVectors.details: Limited domestic revenue leaves infrastructure and energy projects reliant on foreign aid, Gulf partners, and international lenders, reducing bargaining power over strategic assets.

frictionVectors.title: Mining concessions and strategic minerals
frictionVectors.details: Copper and cobalt production remains tied to foreign capital, processing capacity, and opaque contracting, limiting the state's share of value from strategic resources. Chinese firms retain major influence while Western and Gulf actors seek alternatives.

frictionVectors.title: M23 conflict and regional interference
frictionVectors.details: Conflict in the east continues to weaken Kinshasa's control over territory, transport corridors, and mineral zones. Rwanda, regional armed groups, and external security interests complicate sovereignty and supply-chain security.

frictionVectors.title: Hydrocarbon concentration
frictionVectors.details: The economy remains heavily dependent on offshore oil, exposing fiscal policy and sovereign bargaining power to foreign operators and volatile prices. Local value addition and diversification remain limited.

frictionVectors.title: Infrastructure and debt exposure
frictionVectors.details: Chinese participation in roads, public works, and resource-linked projects provides essential infrastructure but can narrow fiscal and procurement autonomy. Debt-service pressures constrain the government's room to renegotiate terms.

highlights: Abidjan emerges as a regional logistics hub

frictionVectors.title: Cocoa value-chain dependence
frictionVectors.details: Côte d'Ivoire remains exposed to foreign processors, traders, and price-setting mechanisms despite efforts to expand domestic grinding and farmer support. Climate stress adds pressure to control over the sector.

frictionVectors.title: Competing infrastructure influence
frictionVectors.details: French, Chinese, Gulf, and multilateral actors compete across ports, transport, energy, and mining. This expands financing options but creates risks of fragmented standards and long-term concession dependence.

highlights: Port network remains a strategic chokepoint

frictionVectors.title: Foreign military footprint
frictionVectors.details: U.S., Chinese, French, Japanese, and other military facilities generate revenue and deterrence but make Djibouti highly exposed to great-power rivalry. Security partnerships can limit independent foreign-policy maneuver.

frictionVectors.title: Port concessions and debt pressure
frictionVectors.details: Djibouti's ports and logistics corridors are central to regional trade, yet concession disputes and debt linked to major infrastructure projects constrain sovereign control. Competition with Ethiopian routes adds commercial and strategic pressure.

frictionVectors.title: External financing dependence
frictionVectors.details: IMF-linked reforms and large Gulf investments provide liquidity but constrain policy space and increase foreign influence over strategic assets.

frictionVectors.title: Red Sea and Suez disruption
frictionVectors.details: Regional conflict and maritime insecurity threaten Suez Canal revenues, energy imports, and Egypt's wider logistics position.

frictionVectors.title: Hydrocarbon depletion
frictionVectors.details: Maturing offshore fields and weak diversification reduce sovereign revenue, leaving the state dependent on foreign operators and volatile energy markets.

frictionVectors.title: Chinese infrastructure exposure
frictionVectors.details: Chinese-built infrastructure and financing remain important, while opaque contracts and debt exposure limit domestic control over strategic projects.

frictionVectors.title: Regional militarization
frictionVectors.details: Eritrea's position along the Red Sea and its involvement in regional security dynamics expose ports and borders to rivalry involving Ethiopia, Gulf actors, and international powers.

frictionVectors.title: Foreign mining dependence
frictionVectors.details: Mining revenues and technical capacity rely heavily on foreign partners, creating leverage over a tightly controlled but economically constrained state.

frictionVectors.title: South African dependence
frictionVectors.details: Trade routes, electricity, finance, and industrial inputs remain closely tied to South Africa, limiting Eswatini's room for autonomous infrastructure policy.

frictionVectors.title: Political legitimacy pressure
frictionVectors.details: Political tensions and governance criticism can deter investment and complicate efforts to secure external financing for energy, water, and logistics projects.

frictionVectors.title: Nile basin confrontation
frictionVectors.details: The Grand Ethiopian Renaissance Dam improves domestic power leverage but continues to generate acute disputes with Egypt and Sudan over filling, operations, and water security.

frictionVectors.title: Port and corridor vulnerability
frictionVectors.details: Landlocked Ethiopia depends on external corridors, especially through Djibouti, while tensions with Somalia and Eritrea complicate its pursuit of more diversified Red Sea access.

frictionVectors.title: Manganese and mining-control renegotiation
frictionVectors.details: The government is seeking greater domestic processing, fiscal returns, and state leverage over manganese and other mineral assets. This creates friction with established foreign operators and financiers.

frictionVectors.title: Port and rail dependency
frictionVectors.details: Export capacity remains concentrated around foreign-linked port, rail, and logistics systems. Any push to restructure these arrangements could affect investment and mineral-export reliability.

frictionVectors.title: External financing and infrastructure leverage
frictionVectors.details: Roads, energy, ports, and digital infrastructure depend heavily on foreign donors, lenders, and contractors. The government has limited bargaining power when financing conditions or strategic access are attached.

frictionVectors.title: Cashew and fisheries vulnerability
frictionVectors.details: The economy remains exposed to external buyers and regional trade disruptions in cashews and fisheries. Weak enforcement also leaves coastal resources vulnerable to foreign overfishing.

frictionVectors.title: Illegal mining and environmental loss
frictionVectors.details: Galamsey continues to damage rivers, farmland, and public trust while exposing gaps in state enforcement. Gold-sector formalization is central to retaining more value domestically and limiting illicit external networks.

frictionVectors.title: Debt, energy, and critical-mineral bargaining
frictionVectors.details: Fiscal restructuring and power-sector liabilities constrain policy autonomy. Emerging interest in lithium and other minerals is increasing pressure to secure stronger local-processing and revenue terms.

highlights: Junta balances control with investor capital

frictionVectors.title: Simandou corridor and foreign consortium leverage
frictionVectors.details: The railway, port, and mine system gives foreign-led consortia substantial influence over Guinea's largest prospective export stream. Conakry is seeking infrastructure and domestic-content gains while avoiding delays that could weaken investor confidence.

frictionVectors.title: Bauxite contract and political-control risk
frictionVectors.details: The authorities are tightening scrutiny of bauxite concessions and demanding greater state participation. The military-led political order creates uncertainty over contract continuity, sanctions exposure, and long-term governance.

highlights: Fragile state amid regional security pressure

frictionVectors.title: Cashew trade capture
frictionVectors.details: The economy relies heavily on raw cashew exports, leaving producers and the state vulnerable to foreign buyers, price swings, and limited domestic processing. This structure captures little value locally and weakens fiscal sovereignty.

frictionVectors.title: Port, narcotics, and political instability
frictionVectors.details: Bissau's weak institutions and strategic Atlantic position create exposure to transnational trafficking networks and external political influence. Port modernization and security assistance can improve connectivity but may also deepen dependency without stronger oversight.

frictionVectors.title: External Debt and Strategic Assets
frictionVectors.details: Debt-service pressures continue to narrow Nairobi's policy space, especially around transport and energy infrastructure financed by external partners. Kenya is seeking greater local control without disrupting critical foreign capital flows.

frictionVectors.title: Lamu Corridor Security
frictionVectors.details: The Lamu Port-South Sudan-Ethiopia corridor remains strategically important but exposed to insecurity, regional competition, and uneven commercial viability. Foreign investment and security assistance remain central to its development.

frictionVectors.title: Lesotho Highlands Water Project
frictionVectors.details: Water exports to South Africa provide vital revenue but bind Lesotho to externally financed infrastructure, contractual asymmetries, and Pretoria's downstream leverage. Delays, cost overruns, and compensation disputes remain sovereignty-sensitive.

frictionVectors.title: Energy and Transport Dependence
frictionVectors.details: Lesotho remains heavily dependent on South African markets, grids, roads, and remittance channels. This limits its bargaining power over infrastructure priorities and resource commercialization.

frictionVectors.title: Iron Ore and Resource Concessions
frictionVectors.details: Large-scale mining investment is central to Liberia's growth strategy but leaves the state exposed to foreign control of deposits, transport corridors, and export logistics. Local-content enforcement and revenue transparency remain key sovereignty tests.

frictionVectors.title: Monrovia Port Competition
frictionVectors.details: Foreign operators and investors hold significant influence over port modernization and shipping access. Liberia must balance concession revenue and infrastructure upgrades against long-term control of a critical national gateway.

frictionVectors.title: Competing Control of Oil Infrastructure
frictionVectors.details: Rival political and armed networks continue to contest authority over terminals, fields, budgets, and the National Oil Corporation. Production stability remains vulnerable to blockades and elite bargaining.

frictionVectors.title: Turkey-Russia and Regional Leverage
frictionVectors.details: Foreign military, security, and commercial relationships give outside powers influence over Libya's ports, energy assets, and political factions. The absence of unified national institutions limits sovereign control over strategic infrastructure.

frictionVectors.title: Mining Concessions and Local Consent
frictionVectors.details: Nickel, cobalt, ilmenite, and other mineral projects attract substantial foreign investment while generating recurring disputes over land, taxation, environmental damage, and local benefit-sharing. Weak state capacity reduces Madagascar's negotiating leverage.

frictionVectors.title: Port and Energy Bottlenecks
frictionVectors.details: Mining and agricultural exports depend on limited ports, unreliable power, and externally financed logistics. Infrastructure gaps allow investors and lenders to shape development priorities more strongly than domestic institutions.

frictionVectors.title: Mining concessions and fiscal dependence
frictionVectors.details: Malawi is courting foreign capital for uranium, rare earths and graphite while trying to improve licensing, taxation and local-benefit rules. Debt distress limits its bargaining power with external financiers and investors.

frictionVectors.title: Fuel and electricity vulnerability
frictionVectors.details: Foreign-exchange shortages, fuel import dependence and unreliable power constrain industrial sovereignty. Regional infrastructure and donor-backed energy projects remain essential to economic stability.

frictionVectors.title: Gold sector confrontation
frictionVectors.details: The junta is tightening control over gold contracts and seeking a larger state share, creating friction with foreign operators and raising concerns about legal predictability. Informal mining and insecurity continue to undermine effective sovereign control.

frictionVectors.title: Security dependence on Russia
frictionVectors.details: Russian military support has replaced much of the former French security role, but this dependence brings opaque agreements, civilian-protection concerns and potential leverage over strategic resources. The breakdown of regional cooperation further limits Bamako's options.

frictionVectors.title: Foreign-led resource megaprojects
frictionVectors.details: Offshore gas, iron ore and prospective green-hydrogen projects are dominated by international partners, making contract transparency and domestic value capture central sovereignty concerns. Infrastructure gaps constrain local participation.

frictionVectors.title: Migration and security bargaining
frictionVectors.details: Mauritania's cooperation with the European Union on migration and Sahel security brings financing and diplomatic leverage but can narrow policy autonomy. Border insecurity and regional instability remain persistent infrastructure risks.

frictionVectors.title: Chagos implementation and base access
frictionVectors.details: Mauritius has strengthened its sovereignty claim over the Chagos Archipelago, but implementation arrangements involving the United Kingdom and continued foreign military access remain politically sensitive. The issue tests the practical limits of national control.

frictionVectors.title: Indian Ocean strategic competition
frictionVectors.details: India, China, Gulf states and Western partners compete for influence through ports, digital infrastructure and maritime cooperation. Mauritius benefits from diversification but must avoid excessive dependence on any single external partner.

frictionVectors.title: Western Sahara resource diplomacy
frictionVectors.details: Morocco is expanding ports, roads, renewables and phosphate-linked activity in Western Sahara, strengthening its physical control while provoking opposition from the Polisario Front and Algeria. Foreign recognition and investment remain politically contested.

frictionVectors.title: External capital in strategic sectors
frictionVectors.details: European, Gulf, Chinese and American investment supports renewable energy, automotive, logistics and water infrastructure. Rabat retains substantial state direction, but external financing creates exposure to geopolitical conditionality and supply-chain dependence.

highlights: LNG revival remains central to fiscal recovery
Cabo Delgado security still conditions sovereignty

frictionVectors.title: LNG enclave dependence
frictionVectors.details: Foreign-led gas projects dominate expected export earnings, limiting domestic control over financing, technology, and revenue timing. Any restart remains vulnerable to militant attacks and security guarantees involving external partners.

frictionVectors.title: Cabo Delgado logistics corridor
frictionVectors.details: Insurgency continues to threaten roads, ports, and energy infrastructure. Reliance on regional and international security assistance exposes gaps in Mozambique's autonomous control of its northern territory.

highlights: New oil and gas leverage is expanding

frictionVectors.title: Frontier hydrocarbons
frictionVectors.details: International oil majors bring capital and technical capacity to offshore discoveries, while Namibia seeks stronger local participation and fiscal terms. The main risk is becoming an export platform with limited domestic value addition.

frictionVectors.title: Green hydrogen infrastructure
frictionVectors.details: Large projects depend on foreign finance, electrolyzer technology, and export corridors. Windhoek retains substantial negotiating leverage but must prevent long-term concessions from narrowing future policy space.

highlights: Junta asserts control over strategic commodities

frictionVectors.title: Uranium and mining renegotiation
frictionVectors.details: Niamey is seeking greater state control and revised terms in uranium and other mining assets, reducing longstanding French influence. The shift risks lower investment and operational disruption if replacement partners cannot provide equivalent expertise.

frictionVectors.title: Oil pipeline dependence
frictionVectors.details: Crude exports depend on the cross-border pipeline to Benin, creating strategic exposure to diplomatic disputes and regional sanctions. Russian security ties may offset some pressure but do not replace commercial infrastructure access.

frictionVectors.title: Upstream investment and production decline
frictionVectors.details: International operators remain important for deepwater capital and technology, while insecurity, theft, and regulatory uncertainty constrain national output. Nigeria's bargaining position improves only if it converts domestic refining and gas capacity into reliable export leverage.

frictionVectors.title: Critical infrastructure insecurity
frictionVectors.details: Pipeline vandalism, crude theft, and attacks on transport links continue to divert public resources and weaken effective control over energy assets. Private security and foreign technical dependence add further sovereignty costs.

highlights: Mineral diplomacy is tied to regional security

frictionVectors.title: 3TG mineral scrutiny
frictionVectors.details: Rwanda's role in regional mineral supply chains attracts international scrutiny over the provenance of tin, tantalum, and tungsten linked to eastern DRC conflict dynamics. Compliance pressure could raise costs and constrain Kigali's commercial and diplomatic maneuverability.

frictionVectors.title: External security partnerships
frictionVectors.details: Foreign aid, investment, and security cooperation remain important to Rwanda's development model and regional operations. These relationships strengthen state capacity but create leverage for donors and partners over conflict policy and governance.

highlights: Maritime security and Gulf of Guinea partnerships deepen

frictionVectors.title: UNTESTED OFFSHORE HYDROCARBON PROMISE
frictionVectors.details: Exploration interest has not yet translated into commercially proven reserves or sustained public revenue. The government faces pressure to protect licensing transparency and avoid overreliance on speculative oil income.

frictionVectors.title: EXTERNAL LEVERAGE OVER PORT AND MARITIME SECURITY
frictionVectors.details: Portugal, China, and Gulf-linked actors compete for influence around port access, logistics, and maritime security. Limited state capacity makes infrastructure agreements particularly sensitive to sovereignty concerns.

highlights: Oil and gas production strengthens bargaining power

frictionVectors.title: HYDROCARBON CONTRACT AND LOCAL-CONTENT PRESSURE
frictionVectors.details: New offshore production is increasing fiscal space, but the government is pushing for greater domestic participation and tougher scrutiny of legacy agreements. Disputes over revenue allocation and contract terms could unsettle foreign operators.

frictionVectors.title: PORT AND LOGISTICS COMPETITION
frictionVectors.details: Dakar's strategic infrastructure attracts European, Chinese, Turkish, and Gulf-linked capital. Financing and operating arrangements create continuing concerns about debt exposure, strategic dependence, and control of critical logistics.

highlights: Debt and fisheries remain external pressure points

frictionVectors.title: FISHERIES ACCESS AND MARITIME SURVEILLANCE
frictionVectors.details: Foreign fishing access and enforcement remain central to the islands' resource security. Seychelles seeks stronger control over its exclusive economic zone while relying on external partners for surveillance and maritime capacity.

frictionVectors.title: STRATEGIC COMPETITION IN THE INDIAN OCEAN
frictionVectors.details: India, China, European states, and Gulf actors compete for diplomatic and maritime influence. Victoria is attempting to preserve room for maneuver while avoiding dependence on any single infrastructure or security partner.

highlights: Mining expansion brings revenue but limited control

frictionVectors.title: IRON ORE AND MINERAL VALUE-CHAIN DEPENDENCE
frictionVectors.details: Large-scale iron ore, rutile, and other mining operations remain strongly shaped by foreign capital, export markets, and logistics providers. The state is seeking more fiscal and local benefits without disrupting investment or production.

frictionVectors.title: PORT, RAIL, AND FINANCING LEVERAGE
frictionVectors.details: Foreign-backed transport and port infrastructure can improve export capacity but may constrain policy autonomy through concession terms and debt obligations. Contract transparency and environmental impacts remain politically sensitive.

highlights: Sovereignty competes with fragmented security authority
Ports and offshore resources attract rival patrons

frictionVectors.title: PORT ACCESS AND REGIONAL RIVALRY
frictionVectors.details: Turkey, the United Arab Emirates, Gulf actors, and neighboring states maintain competing interests in Somali ports and security infrastructure. These partnerships provide essential support but can fragment national authority and constrain federal control.

frictionVectors.title: OFFSHORE OIL AND RESOURCE GOVERNANCE
frictionVectors.details: Exploration and licensing are advancing amid unresolved federal-regional tensions and weak regulatory capacity. Resource competition risks worsening political fragmentation before commercially significant production is established.

frictionVectors.title: Mining sovereignty versus foreign capital
frictionVectors.details: South Africa is seeking greater domestic beneficiation and control over strategic minerals while relying on multinational capital, technology, and export markets.

frictionVectors.title: Energy and logistics constraints
frictionVectors.details: Electricity reliability, port congestion, and rail failures weaken sovereign control over mineral exports and increase dependence on external infrastructure and financing.

frictionVectors.title: Pipeline dependence through Sudan
frictionVectors.details: South Sudan's oil exports remain dependent on infrastructure crossing Sudan, exposing revenue flows to conflict, political bargaining, and disruption.

frictionVectors.title: External security and aid dependence
frictionVectors.details: International peacekeeping, humanitarian financing, and neighboring-state mediation remain central to state stability, constraining independent resource governance.

frictionVectors.title: Competing control of gold corridors
frictionVectors.details: The war economy around gold, border trade, and mining zones is shaped by rival armed networks and foreign commercial links, reducing national control over revenues.

frictionVectors.title: Port and oil infrastructure vulnerability
frictionVectors.details: Conflict threatens Port Sudan and remaining energy infrastructure, while external military, financial, and logistical support influences access to strategic assets.

frictionVectors.title: Mining terms and beneficiation pressure
frictionVectors.details: Tanzania is tightening oversight of gold and critical-mineral projects and pressing for local processing, creating friction with foreign investors over taxation, ownership, and export rules.

frictionVectors.title: Strategic corridor competition
frictionVectors.details: Rail, port, and energy projects attract competing Chinese, Gulf, Western, and regional interests, giving Tanzania leverage but increasing exposure to external bargaining.

frictionVectors.title: Port dependence and external finance
frictionVectors.details: Lomé's role as a Gulf of Guinea logistics hub relies heavily on foreign shipping, construction, and finance networks, limiting domestic control over strategic infrastructure.

frictionVectors.title: Phosphate governance and processing
frictionVectors.details: Togo retains formal control over phosphate resources but captures limited downstream value, leaving the sector exposed to foreign technology, markets, and investment conditions.

frictionVectors.title: EU Financing and Migration Bargain
frictionVectors.details: European financial support and migration cooperation give the EU significant leverage over Tunisian policy. Delays in external financing increase pressure on public finances and strategic imports.

frictionVectors.title: Energy Import Dependence
frictionVectors.details: Tunisia remains vulnerable to imported energy costs and electricity interconnection dependence, especially through its relationship with Algeria and planned links to Europe.

frictionVectors.title: EACOP Financing and Sanctions Pressure
frictionVectors.details: The oil pipeline project with Tanzania is central to Uganda's resource strategy but faces environmental opposition, financing constraints, and Western political pressure. Delays could reduce Kampala's control over project timing and revenue expectations.

frictionVectors.title: Strategic Debt Exposure
frictionVectors.details: Chinese-backed transport and energy infrastructure has expanded Uganda's capacity while increasing repayment and procurement dependence. Fiscal stress could constrain future bargaining power over strategic assets.

frictionVectors.title: Critical Minerals Competition
frictionVectors.details: Copper and cobalt have made Zambia a target for competing Chinese, Western, and Gulf investment. The government is seeking greater local value addition, but foreign capital still dominates financing, technology, and market access.

frictionVectors.title: Power Supply Bottleneck
frictionVectors.details: Electricity shortages and hydropower vulnerability constrain mining output and industrial sovereignty. Emergency imports and grid investment can deepen dependence on neighboring suppliers and external financiers.

frictionVectors.title: Foreign Control of Critical Minerals
frictionVectors.details: Chinese firms remain prominent in lithium and other mineral projects, while the state is attempting to force more domestic processing and capture greater rents. Limited capital and technology leave Harare reliant on external partners.

frictionVectors.title: Currency and Sanctions Constraint
frictionVectors.details: Currency instability, restricted access to international finance, and continuing sanctions-related friction weaken the government's ability to fund infrastructure independently. Resource exports therefore remain central to securing hard currency and external partnerships.
